patient_name: OET role-play — taxi driver after a heart attack, dismissive about lifestyle change and cardiac rehab
chief_complaint: Before discharge, explore a self-employed taxi driver's plan to return to work next week, explain driving restrictions and cardiac rehabilitation, and motivate lifestyle change

team_brief.title: After a heart attack: a taxi driver who wants to be back at work next week
team_brief.patient: Mr Emmanuel Boateng, 52-year-old self-employed taxi driver, four days after a heart attack treated with a stent
team_brief.location: Cardiac ward; you are the nurse preparing Mr Boateng for discharge tomorrow
team_brief.situation: Mr Boateng had a heart attack four days ago and had one stent put in a blocked heart artery. He is due to go home tomorrow. He has told another nurse that he 'feels fine now' and plans to be back driving his taxi next week. He has not agreed to be referred to cardiac rehabilitation.
background: He smokes about 20 cigarettes a day, drives 10-12 hours a day, and usually eats takeaway food between fares.
He is overweight, has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and does little exercise.
He is married with two teenage children; he is the main earner.
current_status: Recovering well: no chest pain since the stent, walking around the ward independently.
Started on new heart medicines, including blood-thinning tablets, which he must not stop without medical advice.
key_data: The stent opened one blocked artery, but the disease that caused the blockage (fatty build-up in the arteries) is still present, so the risk of another heart attack remains unless risk factors change.

Cardiac rehabilitation: a programme of supervised exercise, education and support, usually starting soon after discharge, typically one or two sessions a week for several weeks, at different times of day, with some online or home-based options. It lowers the chance of another heart attack and helps people return to work with confidence.
Stopping smoking is the single most effective change he can make; support and nicotine replacement are available.

Driving: the cardiologist has advised he must not drive his taxi for work until he is cleared at his follow-up review. Rules for professional drivers after a heart attack are stricter than for private drivers, and he must check with the authority that licenses him. Rules for driving his own car also vary by country; he should check with the team before driving at all, and may need to tell his vehicle insurer.
If loss of income is a worry, the team can refer him to a social worker or welfare advice service for information on financial support.
treatments: Already done: stent to one coronary artery; new medicines started.
Pending: cardiology follow-up; referral to cardiac rehabilitation and a stop-smoking service if he agrees.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Mr Boateng's plans and concerns, explain why he cannot return to taxi driving yet, and encourage him to join cardiac rehabilitation and make lifestyle changes.
must_include: Find out Mr Boateng's plans for returning to work and what is worrying him about time off.
Explain in simple terms why the stent does not remove the need for lifestyle change, especially stopping smoking, and offer support.
Explain that he must not drive his taxi for work until he is cleared, and advise him to contact his licensing authority.
Explain what cardiac rehabilitation involves and persuade him to accept a referral.

kickoff_text: Ah, you're the one with the leaflets. Look, I appreciate it, but the stent's in, I feel great. I'll be back in the cab next week.
persona_override: You are Emmanuel Boateng, a 52-year-old self-employed taxi driver, four days after a heart attack treated with a stent. You are cheerful, confident and a joker, and you use humour to avoid thinking about what happened. Your specific resistance: you believe the stent has 'fixed' your heart, so rehab and lifestyle change are unnecessary, and 'rehab is for old men in tracksuits'. Underneath, your real worry is money: you are self-employed, you have no sick pay, your car loan payment is due, and your family depends on you; you are also more frightened by the heart attack than you admit. Ground truth: you smoke about 20 a day and have tried to stop once; you drive 10-12 hours a day; you eat takeaway between fares; you have high blood pressure and cholesterol; you had crushing chest pain while waiting at a taxi rank and a passenger called the ambulance; you are married with two teenagers; you did not know there are rules about driving a taxi after a heart attack; you did not know rehab can be at flexible times or partly at home. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences, and use light humour. If the nurse uses words like 'myocardial infarction', 'PCI', 'coronary artery disease', 'secondary prevention', 'atherosclerosis' or 'DAPT' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse lectures you about smoking or diet without asking about your situation, brush it off: 'Everyone's got to die of something.' If the nurse never asks why you want to go back so soon, bring it up again, more seriously: 'You don't get it. If I don't drive, we don't eat.' If the nurse acknowledges your money worries and asks about them, drop the jokes and admit the heart attack scared you. If the nurse explains that the stent fixed one blockage but the same process is still going on in your arteries, become more thoughtful: 'So it could happen again?' Accept rehab gradually: first ask 'How many times a week?', then agree when you hear it is flexible. React with genuine surprise to the driving restriction ('Nobody told me that!'), and ask 'Who do I even tell?' If the nurse offers stop-smoking support, say you will 'give it a go' but ask about nicotine patches. Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: agree to the rehab referral and the stop-smoking service, say you will check the driving rules, and thank the nurse with a joke.
learning_objectives: find out the patient's plans for work and his worries about money and time off
explain that the stent fixed one blockage but the artery disease is still there
explain he must not drive his taxi until cleared and should contact the licensing authority
explain what cardiac rehabilitation involves and that sessions can be flexible
advise that stopping smoking is the most important change and offer support
check understanding and summarise the next steps
suggested_questions: It sounds like getting back to work is really important to you. Can you tell me what's worrying you about taking time off?
The stent has opened up the one artery that was blocked, but the fatty build-up that caused it is still in your arteries. That's why what happens next really matters.

I need to let you know that the cardiologist has advised you not to drive your taxi until you've been checked at your follow-up. The rules for professional drivers are stricter, so it's important you contact the authority that licenses you.
Cardiac rehab isn't just a gym class — it's exercise, advice and support, and the sessions can often fit around your life. Would you be happy for me to refer you?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Secondary prevention and return to work after myocardial infarction in a professional driver
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NICE NG185 (acute coronary syndromes), NICE CG172 (secondary prevention after myocardial infarction), British Heart Foundation cardiac rehabilitation information and national driver-licensing medical standards; driving and return-to-work rules follow the relevant licensing authority and cardiology advice
core_concepts: A stent treats the culprit lesion but not the underlying coronary artery disease; secondary prevention (medicines, smoking cessation, diet, activity) reduces the risk of further events.
Cardiac rehabilitation improves outcomes and quality of life after myocardial infarction, yet uptake is low, especially among working-age men and the self-employed.
Professional drivers are subject to stricter medical licensing standards after acute coronary syndrome than private drivers.
diagnostic_clues: Humour and 'I feel fine' can mask fear and financial pressure; asking about work and money often reveals the real barrier.
Early wish to return to demanding work may signal financial need rather than lack of understanding.
common_misconceptions: Cardiac rehabilitation is only for elderly or very unfit patients.
If there is no chest pain, it is safe to stop the new medicines.
dangerous_errors: Telling the patient he can return to professional driving next week, or not mentioning driving restrictions at all.
Suggesting he can stop blood-thinning or other heart medicines once he feels well.
Moralising about smoking and lifestyle, which tends to end engagement.
management_principles: Explore the patient's plans, beliefs and practical barriers first.
Explain the disease process simply, then link rehab and lifestyle change to what matters to him (work, family).
Be clear about driving restrictions, offer referrals (rehab, stop-smoking service), and summarise next steps.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Driving restrictions after a heart attack, especially for taxi and other professional licences, differ between countries and licensing authorities; the nurse should advise the patient to check rather than quote a specific period.
Timing of cardiac rehabilitation, return to work and physical activity is individualised and follows cardiology advice and local programmes.
Medicines and their duration (for example, dual antiplatelet therapy) follow the prescription; financial support options for the self-employed vary by country.
